A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cosmic ray ionization rate in molecular clouds, and in particular in molecular cloud cores and protostellar envelopes, is likely dominated by a low energy component of cosmic-ray electrons and/or cosmic-ray protons, which is not directly observable from the Earth.
the ionization rate is not a good tracer of the cosmic-ray flux.

the ionization rate is not the only factor that affects the chemical evolution of molecular clouds, and that other processes like the formation of dust grains, the freeze-out of species, and the photodissociation by UV photons should also be included in the chemical models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the low-energy cosmic-ray flux in the local inter-stellar medium is not yet constrained and should be considered as a free parameter in models of molecular cloud ionization.

the cosmic-ray ionizing flux is a function of the local environment and that the local cosmic-ray ionization is a key quantity to be measured in order to understand the chemistry and physics of molecular clouds.

the ionization rate is not a unique function of the column of material traversed by cosmic-ray particles, and the ionization rate of molecular clouds is not simply proportional to the ionization rates of the diffuse interstellar medium.
